explanations.explanation: Yep, a boat. The crowds got so large that Jesus got into a boat and sat down, while all the people stood on the shore (Matthew 13:2). I think that's a pretty smart spot to teach from. Crowd on the shore, Jesus in the boat.

No mountain here, friend. The text says Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea, and when the crowds got large, He got into a boat (Matthew 13:1-2). The people stayed down on the shore. Picture the shoreline packed and Jesus out on the water.

A rooftop would be a fun spot, but the text doesn't put Him there. Jesus had just gone out of the house and sat by the sea (Matthew 13:1). When the crowds got large, He got into a boat and sat down. The people stood on the shore (Matthew 13:2).
Birds, that's it. Some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it (Matthew 13:4). Seed just lying out on a path is easy pickings. Nobody had to sneak in, either.

Goats would make a fun story, but Jesus never mentions one. He says some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it (Matthew 13:4). A goat wandering in would be a whole different parable. The answer is birds.

Locusts would be a rough day for any farmer, but that's not in this story. Jesus says the birds came and devoured the seed that fell along the path (Matthew 13:4). Birds come from above and don't need an invitation. Same result, though, because that seed is gone.

I see why you'd think so, since shallow soil sounds like it would hold things back. But the text says the opposite. The seed on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, sprang up quickly because the soil was shallow (Matthew 13:5). So the answer is False.

That's right, it's False. The seed on rocky ground sprang up quickly, and the text says it was because the soil was shallow (Matthew 13:5). Not much soil, not much waiting. That little seedling was in a hurry.

True. Jesus says that when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched (Matthew 13:6). That seed had sprung up quickly because the soil was shallow (Matthew 13:5). Then the sun rose and it did not go well.

It's actually True, friend. Jesus says that when the sun rose, the seedlings were scorched (Matthew 13:6). So the sprouts on the rocky ground did not get a happy ending. The sun that shows up for every seed was too much for these.

No root, that's the problem. Jesus says the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root (Matthew 13:6). I've seen cookies that looked great on the tray and fell apart when I picked them up, so I get it. Something was missing underneath.
Rain isn't the problem Jesus names. He says the seedlings withered because they had no root (Matthew 13:6). The sun scorched them, and nothing below held them. Water isn't mentioned.

Shade would have been nice, but that's not what Jesus says. The sun rose, the seedlings were scorched, and they withered because they had no root (Matthew 13:6). A little seedling holding a tiny umbrella is a funny picture, though. Root is the answer.

Choke is the word. Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up and choked the seedlings (Matthew 13:7). The thorns were not sitting there politely. They grew up right alongside the seed and crowded it out.

Shelter would be a kind thorn, and these thorns are not kind. Jesus says they grew up and choked the seedlings (Matthew 13:7). Nothing about them was protecting anybody. Those seedlings were being crowded out.

Strengthen sounds nice, but thorns don't work that way in this story. Jesus says they grew up and choked the seedlings (Matthew 13:7). The seedlings were not helped by the neighbors. They were squeezed.

explanations.answer: Up to a hundred times over
explanations.explanation: A hundred times over, friend. The seed on good soil produced a crop, and Jesus gives three amounts: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold (Matthew 13:8). Even the smallest number there is thirty times what was sown. After three rough patches, this ending is a big one.
Jesus says a lot more than that. The good soil produced a crop, a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold (Matthew 13:8). Those numbers are far past just enough. This crop was big.

That would be a sad harvest, and that's not the story. The seed on good soil produced a crop, a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold (Matthew 13:8). That's much more than what went in, not less. After the path, the rocky ground and the thorns, this ending turns things around.

explanations.answer: Why He speaks to the people in parables
explanations.explanation: Right. The disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Why do You speak to the people in parables?” (Matthew 13:10). They were not asking about the farmer or the seed. They wanted to know why Jesus teaches this way.

explanations.answer: Why He teaches the crowd from a boat
explanations.explanation: The boat was part of the scene, but it's not what they ask. The disciples asked, “Why do You speak to the people in parables?” (Matthew 13:10). Their question was about how He speaks, not where He sits.

explanations.answer: Who the farmer in His story is
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to wonder, but the disciples don't ask it. They ask, “Why do You speak to the people in parables?” (Matthew 13:10). Jesus answers that question first. Notice they're asking about the parables themselves.

True. Jesus says, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you, but not to them.” (Matthew 13:11). He is talking to the disciples there. The word “given” tells me this knowledge came as a gift to them.

It's actually True. Jesus says, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you, but not to them.” (Matthew 13:11). The “you” is the disciples, and the “them” is the people. So the statement matches what He says.

Taken away, that's what Jesus says. “Whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” (Matthew 13:12). It's the other half of the line about whoever has being given more. That one is heavy, so it deserves a slow read.

Doubling isn't the word Jesus uses. He says whoever has will be given more, and he will have an abundance (Matthew 13:12). For whoever does not have, “…even what he has will be taken away from him.” (Matthew 13:12). So the answer is taken away.

Staying the same would be the calm option, but Jesus doesn't say that. “Whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” (Matthew 13:12). So things do change for that person. What he has is taken away.

explanations.answer: They do not truly see or understand
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.” (Matthew 13:13). He then quotes Isaiah, who says they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes (Matthew 13:15). So the reason is that they do not see or understand.

explanations.answer: They have not heard enough stories
explanations.explanation: More stories isn't the reason Jesus gives. He says, “This is why I speak to them in parables: ‘Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.’” (Matthew 13:13). The problem is not how many stories they've heard. It's that they do not hear or understand.

explanations.answer: They are standing too far away
explanations.explanation: The crowd is on the shore and Jesus is in the boat, so I see where you're coming from. But distance isn't what Jesus names. He says, “Though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.” (Matthew 13:13). That's the reason He gives.

Closed is the word. Jesus quotes Isaiah, the prophet, saying, “they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes.” (Matthew 13:15). So the picture is hearts gone callous, ears that hardly hear, and eyes that are shut.

Opened is the opposite of what the prophecy says. Isaiah, the prophet, says of this people, “…they have closed their eyes.” (Matthew 13:15). Open eyes are what the next line is about: “Otherwise they might see with their eyes…” (Matthew 13:15). So closed is the answer.
Lifted sounds hopeful, but it's not in the prophecy. Jesus quotes Isaiah, the prophet, saying, “…they have closed their eyes.” (Matthew 13:15). Closed is the word.

True. The prophecy says, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” (Matthew 13:15). So it names seeing, hearing, understanding and turning, and then healing. That's a door left open.

It's actually True. The prophecy says, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” (Matthew 13:15). Healing is right there in the words. So the statement matches.

explanations.answer: They are blessed because they see and hear
explanations.explanation: That's right. Jesus tells His disciples, “But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.” (Matthew 13:16). After talking about eyes that don't see, He turns to the ones that do. I think that's good news after a heavy stretch.

explanations.answer: They are closed just like the crowd's
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the opposite about His disciples. “But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.” (Matthew 13:16). The “but” marks the turn from the crowd to them. Their eyes and ears are called blessed.

explanations.answer: They will see and hear only much later
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.” (Matthew 13:16). He says they see and they hear. Nothing in the line points to later.

I see why it sounds true, since those prophets were great men. But Jesus says many prophets and righteous men “…longed to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.” (Matthew 13:17). They wanted it and did not get it. So it's False.

Right, it's False. Jesus says many prophets and righteous men “…longed to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.” (Matthew 13:17). They longed for it. The disciples are the ones who get to see and hear it.

The evil one. Jesus says, “…the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. This is the seed sown along the path.” (Matthew 13:19). It's about someone who hears the message of the kingdom but does not understand it. What was sown in his heart gets snatched away.

The Pharisees don't show up anywhere in this passage. Jesus says it's the evil one who comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart (Matthew 13:19). That's the seed sown along the path. So the answer is the evil one.

False prophets aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. Jesus names the evil one, who comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart (Matthew 13:19). It happens to the one who hears the message of the kingdom but does not understand it. I think that's a quiet warning to hold on to what you hear, friend.

True. Jesus says, “The seed sown on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy.” (Matthew 13:20). So the start is happy and it's quick. The trouble comes in the next verse.
It's actually True. Jesus says the seed sown on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy (Matthew 13:20). That's a happy start. The trouble comes after that.

Falls away, that's the one. Jesus says, “But since he has no root, he remains for only a season. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away.” (Matthew 13:21). It matches the seedlings with no root in the sun. The joy was real, but there was nothing below holding it.

Digging deeper is what a root would do, but this one has no root. Jesus says, “When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away.” (Matthew 13:21). So he falls away instead. That's the answer.

Fighting back isn't in the picture here. Jesus says that when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away (Matthew 13:21). This is the one who has no root and remains for only a season. Joy at the start, then gone when trouble shows up.

Unfruitful. Jesus says the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, “…and it becomes unfruitful.” (Matthew 13:22). Remember the thorns that grew up and choked the seedlings (Matthew 13:7)? Same picture, only now it's worries and the deceitfulness of wealth doing the crowding.

Stronger is the opposite of what happens. Jesus says the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, “…and it becomes unfruitful.” (Matthew 13:22). A choked plant gives no crop. That's the answer.

Hidden sounds close, but it's not the word Jesus uses. He says the word is choked by the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth, “…and it becomes unfruitful.” (Matthew 13:22). The point is that no fruit comes. Unfruitful is the answer.

He understands it. Jesus says, “But the seed sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it.” (Matthew 13:23). Back on the path, the one who heard did not understand it (Matthew 13:19). This one hears, understands, and bears fruit.

Memorizing is a fine thing, but that's not what Jesus says here. The one on good soil “…hears the word and understands it.” (Matthew 13:23). I could recite my cookie recipe all day and still burn a batch, so understanding is a different thing. Understanding is the answer.

Repeating is not what Jesus says here. He says the one on good soil “…hears the word and understands it.” (Matthew 13:23). Compare the path, where someone hears but does not understand (Matthew 13:19). So understanding is the answer.
